msgid: Publish your WordPress site as static HTML over SFTP/FTP, HTTPS, Cloudflare or GitHub Pages. Bricks-aware; works with any WordPress content.
Inspect and drive the ShipStatic export/sync engine.

Lock this WordPress site to the addresses below and send everyone else to your static site. Your visitors use the static site, so only editors need WordPress, and a site no stranger can reach can’t be attacked through its plugins, logins or forms.

Opening this link adds the address you’re on to the list, so it gets you back in when your address changes. Anyone who has it can get in, so keep it private, and bookmark it rather than sharing it in public places.
I’ve saved this link somewhere safe
Your address, as this server sees it: %s
A proxy or CDN says your address is %1$s, but the server sees %2$s. The site is probably behind a proxy, so the address it sees may be shared or change. Use the unlock link if you get locked out.
Off: anyone can reach this WordPress site.
Strangers are stopped by .htaccess rules, before any PHP runs.
Strangers are stopped before any PHP file runs (through .user.ini). Changes can take up to 5 minutes to apply; until then WordPress itself blocks them.
Strangers are stopped inside WordPress, before other plugins load. This server offers no way to stop them earlier, so a plugin file opened directly isn’t covered.

A test from this browser without its unlock cookie was turned away. You’re still in for 12 hours thanks to the cookie, but after that you’d be locked out. Add your address, or turn Lockdown off again.
Checked: a stranger is stopped by .htaccess, before PHP runs.
Checked: a stranger is stopped before any PHP file runs.
Checked: strangers are only being stopped inside WordPress. The .htaccess rules aren’t taking effect: this server may ignore .htaccess, or (OpenLiteSpeed) need a restart to read it.
Checked: strangers are only being stopped inside WordPress for now. PHP can take up to 5 minutes to read .user.ini; check again then. If it stays like this, the host ignores .user.ini.
Checked: strangers are stopped inside WordPress.
Couldn’t check: the server’s own address (%s) is on the list, so its test request got in.
A test request without permission got in, so the site isn’t locked. Write the files again.
Lockdown’s files are missing or out of date (another plugin may have rewritten .htaccess).
Making sure Lockdown is working. A server can take a few seconds to read the new rules.

This browser has reached the server from more than one address (%s), as often happens on a mobile connection, so allowing one address won’t keep you in. You aren’t locked out: turning Lockdown on gave this browser a 12-hour pass. Keep the unlock link handy (opening it lets you back in from any address), or allow the range your provider uses. A range lets in everyone on that part of its network, though they still need a WordPress login.

Single addresses (203.0.113.7) or ranges (203.0.113.0/24, 2001:db8::/64). Turning Lockdown on and the unlock link add only the one address in use. IPv6 addresses often change every day, so add your /64 range if you need it.
No addresses yet. Turning Lockdown on adds yours.
Blocked visitors go to the same page on %s.
Blocked visitors see a 403 page (no destination has a Destination URL).
Email the site admin when the unlock link adds an address

Without this, Lockdown covers pages and PHP files only: nginx serves uploaded files (images, PDFs), CSS and JavaScript without running PHP, so anyone with a file’s address can still open it. Most of those are public on your static site anyway, but files uploaded for drafts or private pages are not. If you manage this server, paste this into the site’s server { } block and reload nginx. It holds the list as it is now: after any change, including an address added by the unlock link, paste it again.
Scripts and services can send the same key as a request header instead. It lets that request through without adding its address. New link changes it too.
Unlock key as a request header
If your host only lets cron jobs fetch a web address, send the unlock key with the request:

WordPress’s own WP-Cron runs as usual: the site’s requests to itself always get through. A server cron job (cPanel’s Cron Jobs, crontab) that fetches wp-cron.php over the web with wget or curl, or an online cron service, is turned away like any other visitor, so scheduled tasks stop. Run it with PHP on the command line instead, which Lockdown never stops. If the server can’t find php, use its full path (on cPanel: /usr/local/bin/php).
Allowing the server’s own address works too, but on shared hosting it’s shared by every site on that server, which would let them all past Lockdown.

This site turns off WordPress’s own WP-Cron (DISABLE_WP_CRON in wp-config.php), so scheduled tasks rely on a server cron job. If that job fetches wp-cron.php over the web (wget, curl, an online cron service), Lockdown turns it away unless it sends the unlock key: see “Using a server cron job?”.
Open your unlock link. It adds the address you’re on.
With WP-CLI: wp shipstatic lockdown off, or wp shipstatic lockdown allow <address>.

Over FTP or a file manager: replace everything in wp-content/shipstatic-lockdown.php with just <?php (don’t delete it: PHP needs it while .user.ini points to it), then delete the # BEGIN ShipStatic Lockdown block from .htaccess and the ; BEGIN ShipStatic Lockdown lines from .user.ini. Renaming the plugin folder alone isn’t enough.
Turning ShipStatic off (deactivating it) removes every Lockdown file.
Generate and serve static HTML versions of your site for performance.

Makes the search boxes on your static site work: each sync adds a search index for that destination, searched in the visitor’s browser. The live WordPress site keeps its own search. Press Process after changing this.
Use ShipStatic search on the WordPress site too

The ShipStatic Search element then searches as you type on this WordPress site as well, from the pages in the last Process (press Process to pick up new content). Other search boxes keep normal WordPress search.
How many destinations to upload to at the same time during a multi-destination sync. Higher is faster but uses more connections. Requires WP-CLI; otherwise syncs run one at a time.
Process and Sync automatically on a schedule — the same full sync as the Sync button, to the destinations you pick.
Every enabled destination, including ones you add later.
Pick at least one destination, or turn on All destinations.
Schedules run through WP-Cron, which fires when someone visits the site. On a quiet site a sync can start a little late; a real server cron calling wp-cron.php keeps it on time.
Wiped a remote, or want a full re-upload? Reset clears the push record for every destination.
Controls which pages are discovered and exported.

Export only the pages you choose. Each Page, Post and custom post type gets an "Include" switch — off by default, except the home page — in its editor, the Pages/Posts list and the front-end Sync panel. Nothing else is crawled in, so the export is exactly your selection.

Starts at your home page and follows internal links from page to page. A page that nothing links to isn't reachable by a visitor, so it's left out — this also keeps builder-only URLs (such as Bricks /template/… previews) out of the static site.

Also includes every published page, post and taxonomy archive — even ones nothing links to (orphaned content). Use this if you rely on pages reached only through JavaScript navigation, or deliberately keep unlinked landing pages.
Either way, builder/preview post types are never exported.
Re-render every page. The safe choice: it picks up every change, including menus, templates and site settings.

Re-render only the content added, edited or unpublished since the last Process all, plus the lists that show it and new pages it links to. Site-wide changes (menus, templates, settings) are not checked: use Process all for those.
Every page is rendered again before uploading. Use it after plugin or theme updates, or changes the dashboard can’t see (other plugins’ settings, time-based content).
The current render is up to date, so Sync uploads it straight away without rendering again. Tick Re-render if you changed something the dashboard can’t see.
Content has changed since the last Process, so Sync will render every page first. To render only what changed, use Process changes first.
The render is out of date, so Sync will render every page first.

Sync uploads straight to the destination over FTP, FTPS or SFTP. Enter the connection details, Test, then Save.
A single PHP file you download here and upload to the destination web root once. After that, syncs run over signed HTTPS — no FTP account, and each sync goes up as one package.
Enter the Destination URL above (it must be HTTPS) and Save.
Press Pair, then download the connector file made for this destination only (the link works once).
Upload bs-connector-<id>.php to the folder served at that URL.
Press Test, then Check / Sync as usual.
Needs PHP 7.4+ at the destination; ZipArchive there enables one-package deploys (otherwise files upload one by one).
nginx has its own limits, which PHP (and so the connector) can’t see. Make sure the destination site has at least this:
PHP runs for .php files in the folder the connector is in (a location ~ \.php$ block passing to PHP-FPM, as for any PHP site). Without it, Test reports HTTP 405 or 404.
client_max_body_size of at least 2m. ShipStatic uploads in pieces under 1 MB and retries smaller ones if refused, so nginx’s 1m default works unless it has been lowered.
fastcgi_read_timeout 300s; in that PHP location: unpacking a large site can take longer than the 60-second default.

Cache rules, so browsers recheck pages after a sync. Without a Cache-Control header, browsers guess how long a page stays fresh and can keep showing an old copy for a long time. The nginx snippet on the Destination Server Configuration tab sets HTML to always revalidate and caches assets for a year.
Block public access to .htaccess files and the connector’s in-progress uploads. The nginx snippet on the Destination Server Configuration tab includes the rules.
Paired — expects %s in the destination folder.
Pairing is set by wp-config constants.

Publishes the site to Cloudflare’s global network as a static Worker — no web host, PHP or FTP account needed. Each sync uploads only the files Cloudflare doesn’t already have, then switches the whole site over at once.
In the Cloudflare dashboard, open Workers & Pages and copy your Account ID (shown on the right of the overview).
Create an API token (My Profile → API Tokens → Create Token → Custom token) with the permission Account → Workers Scripts → Edit, limited to that account.
Choose a Worker name for this site (lowercase letters, numbers and dashes, e.g. my-site). It doesn’t need to exist — the first sync creates it.

Press Test. If the Destination URL is empty it is filled with the Worker’s workers.dev address — or enter your own domain once it is attached to the Worker (Worker → Settings → Domains & Routes). Save, then Check / Sync as usual.
Cache headers are published automatically (Cloudflare’s _headers); Cloudflare compresses files itself, so no .htaccess or .gz files are used.
Limits: 25 MiB per file (larger files are left out and reported) and 20,000 files on the Free plan (100,000 on paid plans). Forms that post back to WordPress don’t work on a static copy.
The Destination URL has been set to this address — Save to keep it.

Publishes into a folder on this same server by writing the files directly: no FTP account, Connector or outside service. Use the folder your domain serves (WordPress then lives in a sub-folder such as /wp), or a folder beside WordPress that another domain points at.
Sets up a folder on this server for the static site, checks that its address serves it, and switches this destination to it.

The static site and WordPress will share one domain. That’s the easiest setup, but any third-party script on your public pages (an embed, analytics, a chat widget) then runs on the same domain as wp-admin. If you can set up a subdomain for WordPress, that keeps them apart.

This server runs nginx, which ignores .htaccess. Its configuration must serve this folder at the domain root and pass the WordPress sub-folder to PHP. Ask your host, or use a folder that another domain points at.
A domain or subdomain must point at this folder (in cPanel: Domains, then set its document root). Test checks that it does.
The folder already has files. ShipStatic only ever replaces or removes files it published itself.

You log in again at the new address (login cookies belong to the old one), then run Sync.

Publishes the site to GitHub Pages by committing it to a branch of your repository — no web host, PHP or FTP account needed. Each sync is one commit with only the files that changed.

Most sites keep gh-pages and the whole branch. Change them when the site should live next to your code — for example main with the /docs folder, so your source files at the root are left alone — or for a user or organisation site (a repository named owner.github.io), which usually publishes from main. Pick the same branch and folder in the repository’s Settings → Pages.
Everything in this folder of the branch is replaced by the site on each sync, except CNAME, README, LICENSE and .github/.
Create a repository on GitHub with at least one commit (tick Add a README). Make it public — GitHub Pages on a private repository needs a paid GitHub plan.

Create a fine-grained token (Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token): Only select repositories → this repository, with Contents: Read and write. Optionally add Pages: Read-only so Test can show the Pages status.

Enter the owner, repository and token here. With the default branch gh-pages GitHub turns Pages on by itself at the first sync; for another branch or /docs (under Advanced), choose it afterwards in the repository’s Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch.

Press Test. An empty Destination URL is filled with the Pages address — for a project site https://owner.github.io/repository/, whose /repository/ part becomes the sub-path links are built for. Save, press Process, then Check / Sync as usual.
For a custom domain, set it in the repository’s Settings → Pages (or enter it as the Destination URL); the plugin keeps the CNAME file GitHub uses.

Limits: 25 MiB per file and 1 GB per site. GitHub allows about 500 uploads an hour, so a first sync with many images pauses and carries on by itself. Pages rebuilds at most about 10 times an hour and sets its own cache headers; on a project site robots.txt has no effect. Forms that post back to WordPress don’t work on a static copy.
Re-pairing invalidates the file currently on the destination — upload the new one before the next sync.
Ask the connector what is already on the destination and rebuild the push record from it — so after a reset or re-pair, files that are already there and identical don’t upload again.

No server access needed. Export ZIP packages the current render — with this destination’s replacements applied — into a zip you upload and extract yourself. The plugin uploads nothing and the destination’s sync stats are untouched.
If the pages list is stale, run Process first (Export never renders on its own).
Press Export ZIP and download it when it finishes.

Extract it into the destination web root — the folder served at the Destination URL. If the site lives under a sub-folder, include it in the Destination URL (or, with no Destination URL, set Served from sub-path) before exporting so links are rewritten for it.

The zip includes the .htaccess (Apache/LiteSpeed), .gz siblings where supported, sitemap.xml and robots.txt. On nginx, see the Destination Server Configuration tab for the optional snippet and Check server.
